To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the energy cost of apparent N(2 fixation was constant over the range of acetylene-reducing capacity and (2) the energy cost was the same for all ages and species of the two legumes studied.

the energy requirement per unit of N(2)- fixation is constant, independent of the amount of N(2), fixed, and that the rate of apparent N(2), fixation, in legumes is not limited by the rate of photosynthesis, but is determined by the rate of acetylene, reduction.

(a) the energy cost of apparent N(2 )fixation is constant for different rates of acetyiene reduction, (b) acetylene-reducing capacity in nodules is fully utilized by plants with low rates of apparent photosynthetic CO(2) exchange, and (c) apparent N(2-fixation capacity in alfalfa is not fully utilized by plants at higher rates of CO(2)exchange.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between apparent photosynthesis and apparent N( 2 )-fixation capacity.
the relationship between photosynthesis and N(2)fixation in plants.
the utilization of acetylene-reducing capacity in soybean root nodules and the relationship between acetylene reduction rate and CO(2) exchange rate.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
acetylene reduction is a good measure of N(2)-assimilation capacity in the absence of a direct measure of N(3) fixation.
the energy cost of acetylene-reduced N(2) is 0.453 mg CO(2)/mu mol C(2) H(4).

the acetylene reduction rate of soybean or alfalfa root nodulation is limited by the rate of photosynthesis of the host plant, and the acetylene-reducing capacity of the nodule is not used fully when the CO(2)-fixing capacity of the plant is limited.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the energy cost of apparent N(2), fixation is constant, and the energy cost of respiration is not increased at higher rates of photosynthesis.
apparent N(2 fixation is limited by the availability of photosynthate, not by the capacity to fix N(2) or the energy requirement for N(2)- fixation.
acetylene reduction was not limited by photosynthesis in soybean and that apparent photosynthesis was not limited by acetylene reduction in soybean and in alfalfa.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the energy cost for fixing 1 mole of N2 is about 0.5 moles of CO2, regardless of the plant age or the acetylene-reducing capacity.
acetylene reduction is not a good indicator of the rate of N(2)- fixation in plants with low rates of photosynthesis.
the energy cost of fixing one molecule of N2 is the same for all rates of C2H2 reduction.
